Appendix C Compared Acquisition Rules

Acquisition abbreviations are defined as follows: Bayesian active learning by disagreement (BALD), batch-mode deep active learning (BMDAL), batch active learning via information matrices (BAIT), batch active learning by diverse gradient embeddings (BADGE), largest cluster maximum distance (LCMD), probability of improvement (PI), max-value entropy search (MES), and general-purpose information-based Bayesian optimization (GIBBON). MC denotes Monte Carlo. Table S3 lists the 57 BindingDB configurations under the labels C01-C57 used in the figures; within each row, labels follow the listed rule or coefficient order.

BindingDB has 17 XGBoost (XGB) (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), 29 neural-network (NN), and 11 Gaussian-process (GP) (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006) configurations. The scalar ADMET and joint catalogs add 20 variational Bayesian last-layer (VBLL) configurations (Harrison et al., 2024). Table S3 gives the BindingDB rules and coefficient grids.

The catalog includes CoreSet (Sener and Savarese, 2018), query by committee (QBC) (Seung et al., 1992), and BMDAL (Holzmüller et al., 2023) rules based on information matrices (BAIT), gradient diversity (BADGE), and cluster distances (LCMD) (Ash et al., 2020; Ash et al., 2021). GP rules include probability and expected improvement (Kushner, 1964; Jones et al., 1998), upper confidence bounds (Srinivas et al., 2010), BALD (Houlsby et al., 2011), MES (Wang and Jegelka, 2017), and GIBBON (Moss et al., 2021).

XGB configurations labeled QBC use terminal-leaf identifiers across trees. For candidate xx, let ℓr​(x)\ell_{r}(x) be its identifier in tree rr, v⁡(x)=Varr​[ℓr​(x)]v(x)=\mathrm{Var}_{r}[\ell_{r}(x)] and m⁡(x)=Meanr​[ℓr​(x)]m(x)=\mathrm{Mean}_{r}[\ell_{r}(x)]. Their score is

a⁡(x)=𝒩⁡(v)​(x)+t​𝒩​(m)​(x),a(x)=\mathcal{N}(v)(x)+t\mathcal{N}(m)(x), (4)

where 𝒩\mathcal{N} min-max scales current candidate values to [0,1][0,1], returning one for a constant vector. QBC-diversity (QBCD) adds d​𝒩​(δ)​(x)d\mathcal{N}(\delta)(x), where δ\delta is the minimum distance to labeled and already selected batch members, normalized over remaining candidates. Thus tt weights leaf identifiers, not property predictions; XGB greedy exploitation uses predicted property means. Appendix H.3 tests removal of these twelve leaf-statistic configurations.

NN/VBLL QBC uses the same score with property predictions from MC dropout (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016); mean-only variants rank by raw predictive mean. Within a preselected shortlist, CoreSet and BMDAL hybrids minimize the selection-rule rank plus tt times the greedy-exploitation rank. Coefficients therefore have family-specific meanings. VBLL adds greedy exploitation, random sampling, three CoreSet, three QBC, nine QBC-diversity and three mean-only entries.

GP acquisitions score candidates individually (q=1q=1) and take the highest scores to form a batch. Balanced joint selection adds qEHVI, qNEHVI and qNParEGO (Daulton et al., 2020; Daulton et al., 2021; Knowles, 2006); preference and recommendation comparisons use the 77 scalar configurations.

Appendix D Single-Objective Data Selection: Additional Results

Figure S1(a,b) counts the targets on which each surrogate family and acquisition-rule group ranks first using final-cycle batch mean after seed averaging, with ties resolved in catalog order. Numerical cycle-wise P95 values are in Tables S4 and S5.

D.1 Split Variability and Tied Outcomes

We select the configuration with highest average utility on two campaign splits and evaluate it on the third, rotating the held-out split and resolving ties by catalog order. Regret uses the held-out split’s utility range. Rotations are averaged within target, then across 100 targets. Five-cycle mean averages all 500 acquired observations; five-cycle P95 averages the five batch percentiles.

Two-split selection improves final-batch quality more than five-cycle mean quality. Paired regret differences from XGB greedy exploitation (selected minus XGB) are −0.096-0.096 [−0.144,−0.051-0.144,-0.051], −0.261-0.261 [−0.321,−0.201-0.321,-0.201], 0.0040.004 [−0.0002,0.008-0.0002,0.008] for five-cycle mean, and −0.139-0.139 [−0.183,−0.098-0.183,-0.098] for five-cycle P95. Brackets give descriptive 95% intervals from 10,000 target-bootstrap resamples. XGB’s five-cycle mean regret is already 0.020.

The 57 configurations yield 53 distinct sequences of batch mean/P95 across 1,500 target-seed-cycle combinations. NN greedy exploitation and its three mean-only variants coincide, as do XGB and NN random sampling. Grouping these sequences leaves 34 groups that attain the highest final-batch P95 on at least one target and reduces the mean number within 5% normalized regret from 3.84 to 3.68. Target P01111 has equal P95 for every configuration and regret zero. Tie-aware Hit@1 is unchanged for all 12 main methods with saved lists; Random’s analytic Hit@1 changes from 1.754% to 1.807%. Appendix G.7 extends the analysis to aggregate recommendation utilities across all five settings.

D.2 Complete Cycle Results

GP configurations occupy nine of the top ten positions by five-cycle mean P95 (Tables S4 and S5). GP qUCB (β=8\beta=8) leads at 8.849; GP MES, GIBBON, qUCB (β=2\beta=2), qNEI and qEI are within roughly 0.011 pIC50. The top 20 comprises nine GP, nine XGB and two NN configurations.

Leading GP and XGB configurations tend to acquire high-potency compounds early, with batch P95 declining over later cycles. Several diversity-based XGB and NN configurations improve or remain steadier but have lower five-cycle averages. The best five-cycle mean P95 exceeds the worst by about 0.57 pIC50 and XGB Random by about 0.28.

Appendix E Multi-Objective Data Selection: Additional Results

E.1 Joint Objectives and Component Metrics

Let bib_{i} and sis_{i} denote binding and ADMET desirability, oriented so that higher values are preferred. Predicted XTT toxicity pip_{i} gives si=1−pis_{i}=1-p_{i}; measured endpoints follow Section E.2. Scalar campaigns standardize both objectives using full-pool means and population standard deviations before splitting. Weights are ordered binding/ADMET: balanced acquisition uses (1,1)(1,1) and evaluation (0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5); ADMET-heavy and binding-heavy campaigns use (0.25,0.75)(0.25,0.75) and (0.75,0.25)(0.75,0.25) for both. Each of the 77 scalar configurations runs separately under each preference.

The three multi-objective GP configurations fit one GP per objective, standardized on current labeled data. Their reference point is 0.1 below the smallest standardized labeled value in each objective. The qEHVI and qNEHVI entries use log expected and log noisy expected hypervolume improvement. qNParEGO takes each candidate’s largest log noisy expected improvement over eight random augmented-Chebyshev scalarizations. All three score candidates individually (q=1q=1) and select the highest-scoring batch.

For each batch BtB_{t} on the 90 pools with XTT predictions,

BtNT\displaystyle B_{t}^{\mathrm{NT}} ={i∈Bt:pi<0.5},\displaystyle=\{i\in B_{t}:p_{i}<0.5\}, (5)
T⁡(Bt)\displaystyle T(B_{t}) =100|Bt|∑i∈Bt𝟙[pi≥0.5],\displaystyle=\frac{100}{|B_{t}|}\sum_{i\in B_{t}}\mathbb{1}[p_{i}\geq 0.5], (6)
Q⁡(Bt)\displaystyle Q(B_{t}) =Quantile0.95​{zb​(i):i∈BtNT}.\displaystyle=\mathrm{Quantile}_{0.95}\{z_{b}(i):i\in B_{t}^{\mathrm{NT}}\}. (7)

Here TT is the predicted-toxic percentage and QQ is conditional binding P95, using full-pool standardized binding zbz_{b}. We average batch statistics over five cycles, then three split seeds, then equally across datasets. Scalar P95 instead evaluates every selected molecule’s weighted score wb​zb+ws​zsw_{b}z_{b}+w_{s}z_{s} across all 100 joint pools.

Every main and preference batch contains a predicted non-toxic molecule. In the budget sweep, 33 of 727,650 batches contain none: 23, five, two, two and one at batch sizes 20, 40, 80, 100 and 160, respectively, all with initialization size 200. These batches are omitted from within-seed conditional-binding averages; all batches contribute to predicted-toxic fractions.

E.2 Measured ADMET Endpoints

The ten measured-ADMET pools pair measured endpoints with predicted Boltz-2 binding. Their objectives minimize PXR pEC50, PXR single-concentration log2 fold change, Ames mutagenicity, three Tox21 activity labels, LD50Zhu, LogD and human microsomal clearance, and maximize kinetic solubility. LD50Zhu is a negative logarithm of molar dose, so lower encoded values indicate higher lethal doses. Joint LogD minimization differs from the standalone objective −|y−2|-|y-2|.

ExpansionRx human microsomal clearance is recorded in mL/min/kg (Open ADMET Consortium, 2025). Historical joint prompts mislabeled it as μ\muL/min/mg.

Across all 100 pools, the highest mean scalar P95 is attained by GP qUCB (β=2)(\beta=2) under balanced weights, GP qUCB (β=8)(\beta=8) under binding-heavy weights, and VBLL QBC-diversity (t=10,d=1)(t=10,d=1) under ADMET-heavy weights. These are within-preference comparisons because the utility changes with the weights.

E.3 Dataset-Level Winners and Binding Sources

The seven configurations that rank first most often differ between conditional binding P95 and predicted-toxic fraction (Figure S2). NN configurations receive 48 of 90 dataset wins for conditional binding P95; GP qEHVI receives 27.1 wins for the lowest predicted-toxic fraction. Each dataset contributes one win, divided equally among tied configurations.

E.4 Acquisition Budget Sensitivity

Increasing the initial labeled-set size to 400 or 800 retains all ten leading configurations under conditional binding P95 on the 90 XTT datasets (Table S6).

The seven budget settings use 90 XTT pools and 77 scalar configurations. Fixed-size initialization reshuffles the combined initial and acquisition pools while retaining the diagnostic set. Comparisons therefore use the sweep’s own (200,100)(200,100) reference rather than the main study’s capped-initialization split.

E.5 Binding Metrics and the Binding-Toxicity Pareto Front

Changing the binding statistic changes the binding-toxicity Pareto front (Figures S3 and S4). With balanced acquisition, P90, P85, maximum and mean binding among predicted non-toxic selections yield eight, five, six and twelve Pareto-front entries, respectively; the twelve mean-binding entries occupy six distinct coordinate pairs. GP qEHVI has the lowest predicted-toxic fraction on every front. The highest-binding configuration shifts from NN QBC-diversity for P90/P85 to VBLL QBC-diversity for the maximum and VBLL greedy exploitation for the mean. All panels use the same five-cycle, three-seed, 90-dataset aggregation.

Across the three preferences and 77 scalar configurations, P90, P85, maximum and mean binding yield 14, nine, nine and 22 Pareto-front entries (Figures S5 and S6); the 22 mean-binding entries occupy ten distinct coordinate pairs. ADMET-heavy NN QBC (t=10)(t=10) has the lowest predicted-toxic fraction on every front. The highest-binding entries are GP qEI for P90/P85, VBLL QBC-diversity for the maximum and NN QBC (t=10)(t=10) for the mean. Both acquisition preference and evaluation statistic therefore affect the trade-off.

Appendix F Cross-Property ADMET Study: Additional Results

Assay labels in Table S7 use MDR1 for multidrug resistance protein 1, MDCKII for Madin-Darby canine kidney II cells, Papp for apparent permeability, and A/B for apical/basolateral transport. CYP3A4 denotes cytochrome P450 3A4; EC50 is half-maximal effective concentration, Emax maximal effect, and CLint intrinsic clearance. Prefixes NR and SR denote nuclear-receptor and stress-response assays; AR is androgen receptor, LBD ligand-binding domain, AhR aryl hydrocarbon receptor, ER estrogen receptor, PPAR-γ\gamma peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma, ARE antioxidant response element, ATAD5 ATPase family AAA domain-containing protein 5, HSE heat-shock element, and MMP mitochondrial membrane potential. Potencies pIC50 and pEC50 are negative base-10 logarithms of molar concentrations. Units for E02, E18 and E19 follow the ASAP source assay definitions (Open ADMET Consortium, 2026a).

Table S7 specifies acquisition directions and units. The mouse plasma, brain and gastrocnemius muscle binding objectives maximize percent unbound; their desirability depends on the intended drug profile.

F.1 Endpoint Transfer and Split Variability

Leave-one-endpoint-out selection chooses the configuration with highest mean relative utility on source endpoints. Utilities are normalized over all 77 configurations, with catalog-order ties. The all-endpoint comparison combines continuous P95 and binary inactive fractions after normalization. Within-family comparisons restrict configurations to that surrogate family and sources to endpoints of the held-out endpoint’s type.

For the 22 continuous endpoints, mean rank correlation across split seeds is 0.854 [0.805,0.891] for batch mean and 0.654 [0.592,0.711] for P95; the paired difference is −0.200-0.200 [−0.248,−0.155-0.248,-0.155]. We average the three seed-pair correlations within each endpoint and use 10,000 endpoint-bootstrap resamples for descriptive 95% intervals. At batch size 20, linearly interpolated P95 weights the second-largest observation by 0.95 and the largest by 0.05.

Appendix G Configuration Recommendation: Protocol and Additional Results

G.1 Recommendation Protocol

We compare direct prediction and ICL for Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026c), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026b), and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (Google Gemma Team, 2026). Evaluation covers 100 BindingDB targets, 34 ADMET endpoints and 100 joint pools under each of three preferences.

Both conditions receive the target description, configuration catalog and evaluation objective; ICL adds descriptions and top-15 rankings from the nearest K=20K=20 source datasets. Each model returns five ordered configurations. The task-specific LLM-generated prompt and retrieval rule are fixed before evaluation. Decoding is greedy, with thinking disabled and at most 384 new tokens. Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B use NF4 quantization; the other two models use bfloat16. Supplementary Reproduction contains prompts, checkpoint identifiers and inference settings.

G.2 Held-Out Datasets and Evaluation Utilities

Each collection has a fixed ten-fold partition constructed without outcomes. Every method uses the same held-out fold and the other nine folds as sources: 90 source datasets for BindingDB/joint and 30–31 for ADMET. All preferences of a joint pool stay in the same fold, with source rankings matched to the target preference. Transfer is evaluated within each collection.

Recommendation utilities follow Table S1: BindingDB uses final-batch mean binding; joint tasks use batch P95 of weighted standardized binding/ADMET; ADMET uses oriented P95 for 22 continuous endpoints and inactive fraction for 12 binary endpoints. Joint and ADMET scores average five batches, and all utilities average three split seeds. The recommendation catalogs contain 57 BindingDB and 77 ADMET/joint configurations.

G.3 Descriptions and Retrieval

Descriptions give the dataset identifier, objective and direction, candidate and unique-structure counts, protein length, structural diversity, initialization, batch size and cycle count. Molecular descriptors comprise means of molecular weight, logarithmic partition coefficient (LogP), topological polar surface area (TPSA), hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. They also specify the scoring statistic and cycles, and distinguish joint evaluation weights from acquisition coefficients. Target property values, rankings and normalization constants are excluded.

Molecular similarity is the cosine similarity between mean Morgan fingerprints of unique canonical structures. Protein similarity is the Jaccard similarity between sets of sequence 3-mers. A third term is the square root of the product of the candidate-pool-size ratio and sequence-length ratio, where each ratio is the smaller value divided by the larger. When both sequences are available, the three terms receive equal weights. Otherwise, molecular fingerprint similarity and the candidate-pool-size ratio each receive weight one half.

ICL takes the nearest KK sources. Random retrieval samples without replacement using three source-selection seeds and presents each subset in similarity order. The all-source condition uses the same fixed order for both retrieval methods.

The main comparison contains 3,472 predictions, including 12 invalid Qwen3.5-9B ICL responses. Including source-count ablations gives 24,032 unique predictions and 105 invalid responses, all retained in scoring.

G.4 Scoring, Baselines, and Uncertainty

Let C=|𝒞|C=|\mathcal{C}| and r⁡(c)=1+#⁡{c′:Md,c′>Md,c}r(c)=1+\#\{c^{\prime}:M_{d,c^{\prime}}>M_{d,c}\}, so utility ties receive their best shared rank. Hit@kk (k=1,3,5k=1,3,5) checks overlap between the first kk recommendations and the top kk reference entries, whose utility ties are broken by catalog order. Mean rank averages r⁡(c^1)r(\hat{c}_{1}); BestRk@5 averages minj≤5⁡r⁡(c^j)\min_{j\leq 5}r(\hat{c}_{j}). First-choice regret uses the first entry in the regret equation above. A valid response has five distinct admissible identifiers. Invalid responses receive zero Hit@kk, rank CC for both rank metrics and regret one.

Random reports exact expectations for uniform sampling of five distinct configurations. Its Hit@1 probability is 1/C1/C, and its Hit@kk probability is 1−(C−kk)/(Ck)1-\binom{C-k}{k}/\binom{C}{k} for k=3,5k=3,5; expected ranks account for utility ties. Global Best chooses the five configurations with lowest mean rank across all eligible training-fold sources. Frequency Voting orders configurations by the number of source datasets on which they rank first, counting exact ties, then by mean rank. Most-Similar Source transfers the nearest source’s reference ranking. These methods break remaining ties by catalog order.

K20 rank aggregation averages the same 20 source top-15 lists supplied to ICL: listed configurations receive ranks 1–15 and absent configurations rank 16. It returns the five lowest averages, with catalog-order ties. Every baseline excludes the complete held-out fold.

Predictions are averaged over repetitions within each held-out dataset and then equally across datasets. Confidence intervals use 10,000 held-out-fold block bootstrap resamples, weighting sampled folds by their held-out dataset counts and retaining repetitions within dataset. Paired method differences use the same resampled fold indices. These descriptive intervals summarize variation under the saved cross-validation partition.

G.5 Learned Selectors and Shortlist Diagnostics

Ridge selectors use the same folds and numeric descriptions as the recommendation study: molecular descriptor means, candidate and unique-structure counts, protein length and structural diversity. Counts and protein length use log⁡(1+x)\log(1+x); missing protein length is set to zero with a missingness indicator. Feature standardization and constant-feature removal use only the source datasets for each fit.

All-source ridge predicts complete source ranks scaled to [0,1][0,1]. K20 ridge uses the same 20 top-15 lists as ICL, scaling listed positions 1–15 and censored rank 16 to [0,1][0,1]. Both fit one response per configuration with fixed ridge penalty 10 and an unpenalized intercept. The five lowest predicted scores form the recommendation, with catalog-order ties.

Write first-choice regret as R1​(d)R_{1}(d) and best-list regret as R5​(d)=minj≤5⁡Regret⁡(d,c^d,j)R_{5}(d)=\min_{j\leq 5}\mathrm{Regret}(d,\hat{c}_{d,j}). The ordering gap G⁡(d)=R1​(d)−R5​(d)G(d)=R_{1}(d)-R_{5}(d) measures the loss from choosing the first entry instead of the best entry according to target outcomes. Invalid lists have R1=R5=1R_{1}=R_{5}=1 and G=0G=0.

G.6 Recommendation Results

Tables S8, S9 and S10 report all six recommendation metrics for the five settings. Bold marks tied best point estimates at displayed precision within each reference, direct-prediction or ICL panel.

Supplementary Source Data contains the 40 paired estimates underlying (a,b). Some descriptive 95% intervals include zero: Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it’s binding-heavy Hit@5 gain is 5 percentage points [−7,17-7,17], and all four ADMET first-choice-regret differences between ICL and K20 rank aggregation include zero.

G.7 Sensitivity to Exact Ties and Shortlist Scoring

Tie-aware Hit@kk includes all configurations tied at the reference cutoff. We rescore the original direct and K=20K=20 ICL lists with this rule and with Regret@5.

Including cutoff ties leaves Hit@5 unchanged, and ICL reduces Regret@5 in all 20 model-setting comparisons (Tables S11, S12 and S13). Tie-aware Hit@3 improves in 19 comparisons; Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it on binding-heavy joint selection changes from 37% to 36%.

Grouping configurations with exactly equal aggregate utilities on every dataset yields 53 BindingDB, 69 ADMET and 68 joint groups per preference. Valid ICL lists cover fewer than five groups in 24/136 ADMET, 9/398 balanced-joint, 3/399 binding-heavy and 26/392 ADMET-heavy cases, versus 0/399 BindingDB cases. Every valid direct-prediction list covers five groups. These are post hoc groups of recorded outcomes; primary scores retain the original identifiers. Supplementary Source Data gives the per-model counts and group assignments.

G.8 Source-Count and Retrieval Ablation

Tables S14, S15, S16, S17 and S18 vary source count and retrieval for Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, using the same folds and utilities as the main comparison. The K=20K=20 similarity rows reuse the main predictions. All-source uses 90 BindingDB/joint pools or 30–31 ADMET endpoints. Bold marks tied best values within each setting, model and retrieval group.

Appendix H Additional Configuration-Selection Analyses

Table S19 compares the ridge selectors with K20 rank aggregation; negative differences favor ridge. Table S20 separates first-choice regret into best-list regret and the ordering gap, averaging the four models within target before averaging targets. All analyses use the scoring and fold-bootstrap conventions above.

ICL has lower mean Regret@5 than Global Best in 14 of 20 model-setting comparisons and K20 rank aggregation in eight; its first-choice regret is lower in three and one, respectively. Grouping identical recorded utilities leaves regret unchanged and preserves ICL’s better best-list rank than direct prediction in all 20 comparisons. Gains vary non-monotonically with source similarity: BindingDB first-choice-regret reductions are 0.114, 0.094 and 0.164 across low, middle and high nearest-source-similarity groups. ADMET reductions average 0.143 on binary and 0.111 on continuous endpoints. Supplementary Source Data provides subgroup definitions, counts and paired comparisons.

H.1 Fixed-List Ordering Controls

The controls in Table S21 keep each five-entry list fixed. Uniform ordering has expected first-choice regret equal to the mean regret of its entries. Source reranking sorts entries by their summed positions in the same 20 source top-15 lists used by ICL, assigning absent entries rank 16 and breaking ties by catalog order. Target-fold outcomes are excluded; invalid lists retain regret one.

Original ICL order has lower mean first-choice regret than uniform ordering in 15 of 20 comparisons. Uniform ordering has lower means in the other five, whose paired intervals include zero. Five source-reranking differences have descriptive 95% intervals wholly below zero. Supplementary Source Data also includes direct-prediction and uniform-order paired comparisons.

H.2 Selection across Campaign Splits

For each target, two split seeds select the highest-utility configuration from the catalog or an existing shortlist; the third evaluates it. We rotate the held-out seed and average within target before resampling folds. Regret uses each held-out split’s catalog range, whereas primary recommendation scores use three-seed-averaged utility. Joint diagnostics retain the 77-configuration catalog.

Table S22 compares the two-seed catalog winner and, averaging the four ICL models within target, the original first entry, held-out-best list entry and two-seed-selected list entry. The two-seed gain is the original first-entry regret minus the two-seed-selected regret. Table S23 evaluates source-based and learned selectors’ original predictions under the same held-out-seed scoring.

Near-optimal sets have normalized regret at most ϵ∈{0.01,0.05,0.10}\epsilon\in\{0.01,0.05,0.10\} under each split’s own catalog range. Table S24 reports Jaccard overlap, the fraction of two-seed near-optimal configurations that remain near-optimal (Transfer), and the fraction of rotations in which the two-seed catalog winner is near-optimal (Near-hit).

The two-seed catalog winner has mean held-out regret 0.236 on BindingDB versus 0.330 for Global Best. Global Best has slightly lower means on ADMET and ADMET-heavy joint selection. Near-optimal-set Jaccard overlap at ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05 ranges from 0.152 to 0.260 across settings.

H.3 Catalog Sensitivity

Table S25 removes the twelve XGB leaf-statistic configurations, leaving catalogs of 45 BindingDB or 65 ADMET/joint entries. Original lists are filtered without replacement, retaining zero to five entries; regret uses the reduced catalog’s utility range. Invalid or empty lists receive regret one. This evaluates filtered predictions, not recommendations generated from a reduced catalog.

The excluded configurations account for every original utility maximum on 44/100 BindingDB, 2/34 ADMET, 3/100 balanced, 6/100 binding-heavy and 1/100 ADMET-heavy targets. ICL has lower best-retained-entry regret than direct prediction in 18/20 comparisons; the exceptions are Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on BindingDB. First-excluded counts record removal of the original first choice.

Appendix I Limitations and Responsible Use

Configuration rankings depend on the dataset collection, representations, budgets and source-target split. Predicted XTT scores concern one cell-viability assay; therapeutic safety requires separate assessment. Prospective campaigns also involve assay noise, synthesis constraints and project-specific costs, while measured ADME desirability depends on the endpoint’s screening objective.

Appendix J Data and Code Availability

The five supplementary ZIP archives are available for review at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1I_8AS1szTioU3lcNol2dRiHRXwXhIQaD?usp=sharing. We will replace this review link with a permanent repository link upon acceptance.

Supplementary Inputs contains the candidate tables. Supplementary Raw Results contains campaign archives, recommendation records and associated metadata. Supplementary Source Data supplies figure/table inputs and generation routines. Supplementary Reproduction provides study-specific simulation, recommendation and analysis workflows; Supplementary Software provides the reusable SciSelect-Gym library, documentation, examples and tests.

To regenerate figures and tables or recompute the supplied numerical analyses, start with Supplementary Software, Supplementary Reproduction and Supplementary Source Data. Supplementary Inputs supports campaign reconstruction, and Supplementary Raw Results supports reconstruction of campaign metrics and rescoring of saved recommendations. The raw-results archive contains separately compressed campaign parts that can be read without extracting all simulation records. Package documentation specifies dependencies and the distinction between analysis of saved results and fresh simulation runs.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
